name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: 38 Indiana school districts to seek property tax referendums this fall
description: New restrictions on when school boards can ask voters to raise or renew property tax levies led a record 38 Indiana public school districts to place referendums totaling around $500 million on the November ballot. Public school advocates anticipated anywhere from 45 to 100 districts would pursue referendums to pay for construction, safety or operating […]
text:
Thirty-eight school districts are pursuing referendums in November to pay for construction, safety equipment or operating expenses. (Getty Images)New restrictions on when school boards can ask voters to raise or renew property tax levies led a record 38 Indiana public school districts to place referendums totaling around $500 million on the November ballot.
Public school advocates anticipated anywhere from 45 to 100 districts would pursue referendums to pay for construction, safety or operating expenses this fall due to property tax reforms contained in Senate Enrolled Act 1.
The law, adopted last year, restricts how often school referendums can appear on the ballot to once every two years rather than twice a year.
Districts that declined to pursue additional levies this year won’t get another chance until November 2028.
The deadline to certify a referendum question for the coming election was Aug. 1.
What will appear on the ballot
Seventeen districts are asking voters to renew expiring levies early since they won’t be able to do so next year, according to Terry Spradlin, executive director of the Indiana School Boards Association, which is tracking school referendums.
Six of those districts have levies set to expire in 2027, while the remaining districts are seeking early renewals at adjusted rates, he said.
“Their current rate may not generate the same amount of levy dollars they have been receiving because of the impact of property tax controls,” Spradlin said.
The School City of Whiting is the sole district seeking a construction levy for a $39 million facilities project, though it is also pursuing an operating levy.
Meanwhile, the Wa-Nee Community School Corporation in Elkhart and Kosciusko counties is the sole district pursuing a school safety referendum.
All others are asking to adopt or renew levies for operating expenses like salaries, benefits and supplies.
Spradlin estimated only 10 or so districts are pursuing referendums for the first time — far fewer than expected.
Collectively, the operating levies would generate about $500 million in property tax revenue annually.
Indiana school leaders warn property tax reforms are destabilizing public education budgets

One district — the Eminence School Corporation in Martinsville south of Indianapolis — withdrew its referendum petition from the Indiana Department of Local Government Finance after the school board changed its mind.
Eminence isn’t the only district to decline to pursue a referendum in an election year dominated by backlash to property taxes.
Brownsburg Community School Corporations accepted an $800,000 one-time allocation of tax increment financing from its town council in May in lieu of a referendum.
In addition to the change in when and how referendums can be sought, the Indiana Coalition for Public Education estimates property tax changes contained in SEA 1 will cost public schools $744 million through 2028.
A majority of superintendents surveyed by the coalition last year reported they were considering staff cuts, deferred maintenance and referendums as a result of the law, with some districts already announcing layoffs this year.
“Most districts are reluctant to want to do a referendum because it’s a difficult message to taxpayers,” Spradlin said.
Still, he said a majority of the districts pursuing referendums this year are doing so to maintain the status quo rather than expand on it.
Lawmakers raised the minimum starting teacher salary from $40,000 to $45,000 last year. Meanwhile, Spradlin said the cost of utilities and benefits is outpacing inflation.
“Our expenses are going up while our revenues are not,” he said.
State funding
In related news, State Rep. Gregory Porter, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Ways & Means Committee, called on the State Board of Finance Monday to return $98 million from the state’s general fund to K-12 tuition support.
Porter cited the state’s growing general fund reserves, which reached just shy of $4 billion at the end of June, in his request that the board add a supplemental tuition distribution worth about $100 per student to its August agenda.
Porter - Letter to State Board of Finance - August 2026
“Children are our future, a future Indiana’s not properly funding,” Porter said in statement Monday. “The administration took these dollars while a record number of schools hold referendums. Teachers are being laid off or leaving the profession as Indiana hits $4 billion in savings.”
“Our public schools are fighting to stay afloat,” he said. “They shouldn’t have to wait for the next budget to get relief. The Board has the authority to give that money back to our kids. It’s just a matter of will. I look forward to the Board’s August meeting.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: House set to give final approval to redistricting constitutional amendment
description: A House debate over congressional redistricting — marked by a high level of civility — went on for roughly four hours Monday night, but ended exactly as planned by Democrats, with a proposed constitutional amendment advancing to a final vote Tuesday.
text:
Del. Melissa Wells (D-Baltimore City), chair of the House Government, Labor and Elections Committee, confers with Del. Kris Fair (D-Frederick) during House debate on a bill to set standards for how Maryland congressional districts can be drawn. (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)A House of Delegates debate over congressional redistricting — marked by a high level of civility — went on for roughly four hours Monday night, but ended exactly as planned by Democrats.
The House, in a voice vote, gave preliminary approval to House Bill 2100, the proposed constitutional amendment that would — if passed by the legislature and approved by voters in November — set standards for the state’s congressional districts.
Republicans entered the 2026 special session Monday knowing the outcome is inevitable, with Democrats holding a supermajority in both chambers. The option for Republicans was a fight over amendments — 20 of them over four hours — that stretched the march to a preliminary vote late into the night.
Most proposals were defeated in mostly party line votes. Another half dozen were ruled out of order.
“It’s very difficult to continue doing that,” said House Minority Leader Jason C. Buckel (R-Allegany). “I think every member of our caucus believes firmly that we were elected to represent a constituency who does not want to see the direction Maryland’s going.
“I love Maryland. We are going in a really bad direction. Not just the last two years, the last four years. We’re going in a really bad direction over time,” he said. “I can’t think of hardly anything that’s really going right.”
Advocates, protesters voice frustration over redistricting special session

Adding to Republican frustrations was an edict from House and Senate leaders prohibiting any legislation not related to redistricting from being introduced. They ordered the Department of Legislative Services not to draft those bills.
“We’re here to fight this, we’re here to make noise,” said Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore). “We’re here to make this as uncomfortable as possible for the Democrat supermajority to push through something as partisan as this issue is.”
Hershey, during a morning Senate session, temporarily blocked the introduction of the Senate version of HB 2100 using a rule that requires bills to be delivered to the secretary of the Senate four hours before introduction. The move required the Senate to reconvene in the afternoon to introduce the bill.
Despite limiting the subject matter to redistricting, even some related bills didn’t make the cut.
Del. Christopher Eric Bouchat (R-Carroll) proposed legislation that called for creation of a 188-member body of citizens, elected every 10 years to set legislative and congressional district boundaries after each decennial census.
Bouchat’s bill did not get a hearing.
“My hope was that we could balance out what the Democrats are going to pass with Citizens being sovereign over the redistricting process,” Bouchat said in a text message. “It is just raw partisan politics from the national level having more influence than what is best for Maryland citizens regardless of what part of the state you live.”
Bouchat reverted to his practice at the tail end of the 2026 legislative session: After attending the morning session, he left Annapolis before the debate in the House. He attributed his absence to the decision not to give his bill a hearing.
Republicans planned on using the session to promote bills aimed at affordability issues — high utility prices, car registration fees, gas tax holidays and other issues. They offered those ideas and others in amendment after amendment.
Other amendments attempted to add recent U.S. Supreme Court rulings to the Maryland Constitution, or impose temporary pauses on data centers or related infrastructure.
Del. Thomas S. Hutchinson (R-Lower Shore), right, holds up a flag for a possible new state if the Eastern Shore counties seceded. The proposal was voted down. (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
One proposal, from Del. Thomas S. Hutchinson (R-Lower Shore), called for a vote on secession in the nine Eastern Shore counties.
“The passage of House Bill 2100 will nearly eliminate the possibility of a member of the House of Representatives to reside on the Eastern Shore,” Hutchinson said. “We do not want our representatives — nothing against Howard or Anne Arundel County — but we don’t want them from there because the lifestyle is so different.”
The idea is not new. It was once proposed by Republican Sen. Richard F. Colburn.
Hutchinson held up the flag Colburn had made for the new area he called MarDelVa. Hutchinson said he believed portions of Delaware and coastal Virginia would likely want to join to form their own state.
It was all part of the first day of what could be a three-day session over a bill to overturn a 2022 court decision that hamstrung Maryland lawmakers from joining the national hyper-partisan midcycle congressional redistricting that dominated state legislatures across the country.
The bill proposes amending the Maryland Constitution to get around a 2022 decision by Judge Lynne Battaglia that struck down a 2021 congressional map. Battaglia’s decision cited language in the state constitution that requires districts be compact, contiguous and mindful of jurisdictional and geographic boundaries — language that had always been interpreted to only apply to legislative districts, not congressional districts.
On Monday, House Majority Leader David Moon (D-Montgomery) referred to Battaglia as “an errant judge” and the decision “novel.”
House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) said the bill would return congressional redistricting standards to what was in place prior to 2022.
House Majority Leader Del. David Moon (D-Montgomery). (Photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Members of the House are scheduled to return Tuesday at 9 a.m. for what could be another hour or two of debate and a final vote on the bill. The timing could allow the Senate to hold a preliminary and final vote Tuesday, foregoing the need for a Wednesday session.
The bill must pass by Wednesday to make a deadline to be added to ballots across the state and still meet a certification deadline. Because it’s a proposed constitutional amendment, the measure must go before voters this fall.
Republicans, however, hint at the potential for a legal challenge.
The special session represents a turnaround from earlier this year.
A panel created by Gov. Wes Moore recommended a plan to redraw the congressional districts. The goal was to make the Eastern Shore district represented by Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) more vulnerable to a Democratic challenger.
The proposal sailed through the House but disappeared into the black hole of a rules committee in the Senate. A second bill, similar to that considered Monday night, met a similar fate at the hands of Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore).
In May, Ferguson had a change of heart.
The U.S. Supreme Court gutted parts of the Voting Rights Act and President Donald Trump successfully ousted five Republican state lawmakers in Indiana who had blocked redistricting efforts in that state. Ferguson also faced a tough re-election bid with an upstart primary challenger who adopted the redistricting issue as part of his campaign.
“These acts changed the calculus, and that’s why we’re here,” Ferguson told reporters Monday morning. “During this special session, we are clarifying the rules by which we will draw maps to ensure we are using the standards the state used for decades prior.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“We’ve known that we cannot consider any future map in the near term or the long term without first addressing the uncertainty that the 2022 Battaglia decision created,” he said. “If we want a future legislature to have meaningful options, we must address this issue first, and we have to make sure that Marylanders have a say in that process.”
And while Republicans see the bill as going too far, others believe it doesn’t go far enough.
A coalition of progressive groups rallied outside the State House Monday morning.
“What we’re seeking now is … for the maps to be amended so that the decisions from that governor’s redistricting commission can be added to the legislation and amendment that’s being proposed,” said Daryl Jones, co-leader of the Transformative Justice Coalition.
A map is not expected in this special session, not even from Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) who was a vocal proponent of new maps earlier this year, walking out of a session in protest at one point and later refusing to participate in procedural roll calls to establish a quorum.
Ellis said drawing a map “is a complicated thing.” He said he was happy the legislature had returned to take up the bill to address the Battaglia ruling.
“We’re doing it, right? So I’m happy. I can be pleased,” Ellis said Monday. “It’s not endless discontent.”
— Maryland Matters reporter William Ford contributed to this report.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Is the primary job of SC’s US senator to support Trump? Here’s how 5 candidates answered.
description: COLUMBIA — Questions about the war in Iran and candidates’ general willingness to buck President Donald Trump provided some of the biggest distinctions between Republicans on stage Monday asking South Carolinians to support their bid for U.S. Senate. The winner of the special GOP primary will replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham as the GOP […]
text:
Five Republicans seeking the GOP nomination for U.S. Senate in a special primary participate in the first televised debate Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, at the WIS-TV studio in Columbia. The five (left to right) are former Gov. Mark Sanford, U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, Sen. Darline Graham, and Upstate businessman Mark Lynch. (Screenshot of Gray Media's livestream)COLUMBIA — Questions about the war in Iran and candidates’ general willingness to buck President Donald Trump provided some of the biggest distinctions between Republicans on stage Monday asking South Carolinians to support their bid for U.S. Senate.
The winner of the special GOP primary will replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham as the GOP nominee for November’s general election. The televised debate offered voters statewide a chance to hear from the frontrunners. According to the state GOP, five of its nine certified candidates met the debate’s polling criteria.
The one-hour debate mostly saw the five candidates agreeing with each other. But they differed on whether the senator’s primary job is to support Trump’s agenda.
Two gave a resolute “yes:” Sen. Darline Graham, sister of the late senator; and U.S. Rep. Russell Fry of the 7th District.
Former Gov. Mark Sanford, who in 2019 briefly challenged Trump’s re-election, said his readiness to disagree sets him apart in the crowded field.
U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman and Upstate businessman Mark Lynch were somewhere in between.
It was the first debate for Graham, who was sworn in July 14 to fulfill her brother’s term that ends in January. Not expected to seek the full term, she jumped into the race after Trump simultaneously encouraged and endorsed her campaign.
“This is simple: I completely support the president’s agenda. I’m 100% behind him,” said Graham, of Lexington. “I am honored to have his endorsement.”
Fry, first elected to Congress in 2022 with Trump’s endorsement, also gave an unequivocal “yes.” Many expected Fry to get Trump’s endorsement again.
“The president was elected as commander in chief,” said Fry, a former legislator from the Grand Strand. “He is the coach. It is frustrating for our conservative voters to constantly see people grandstand and jump up and down and oppose him.
“People elected us to do a job,” he continued, adding the president has an “open phone line” to talk through disagreements. “They expect us to get the job done, not grandstand and not get in the way.”
Norman, of Rock Hill, said he supports the president’s agenda and thinks he’s done a great job but said the president likes to hear varying opinions.
“You can disagree with him. He loves competing ideas,” said the 5th District congressman, who flipped his vote for House Speaker Mike Johnson in January 2025 after taking a phone call from Trump on the House floor. “That’s how he makes the final decision. Typically, it’s the right decision.”
Lynch responded “yes,” and noted he voted for Trump every time he was on the ballot, but followed that up with “iron sharpens iron” — that disagreements can bring success.
“I’m not afraid to bring up a question or something I don’t think is right with anybody,” he said. “With that comes the best decisions.”
Sanford, whose last term in Congress was during Trump’s first two years in office, said he thinks the job entails both supporting and disagreeing with the president.
While mostly supporting him, “where I disagree, I have disagreed. And I think that’s the American way,” said Sanford, whose brief presidential run included news conferences across South Carolina with a life-size cardboard cutout of Trump.
“It’s OK to occasionally disagree on things,” Sanford said. That includes getting the authorization of Congress to wage war.
The war in Iran
On whether it was time for the war in Iran to end, Sanford said he applauds Trump’s efforts to wipe out terrorism and prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons. Still, he said, only Congress can declare war.
The last time Congress formally declared war with a country was in 1942, during World War II, according to the U.S. Senate.
But Sanford said his position is personal. As governor, he attended funerals of service members who died. “Body bags don’t go back to Washington,” they go back to service members’ home, he said.
Following the U.S. and Israeli bombing attack launched in February, Lynch blamed Trump’s decision on Lindsey Graham’s influence. On the debate stage, he said he supports Trump as the commander in chief, but “it’s time to bring our men and women home to get them out of harm’s way and get back to what’s important here in America.”
Norman and Fry both said they don’t want “boots on the ground” but believe the mission should be completed.
“Iran needs to be defanged,” Fry said.
Darline Graham sounded much like her brother as she backed Trump and Israel.
“We cannot allow terrorists to build nuclear missiles because they’re going to want to kill Americans,” she said. “The more we can fight them over there and prevent it over there, the better for the United States.”
Differing experience
All five candidates pointed to their backgrounds in their pitches for why they should be the GOP nominee.
In both her opening and closing statements, Graham stressed that she’s “not a politician.” Noting she “grew up in the back of a bar and liquor store,” she said she understands the struggles of average American families.
Fry, the youngest on stage at 41, has drawn a comparison to Lindsey Graham’s humble beginnings. In his opening remarks, Fry said he understands “what it’s like when every dollar mattered because my family lived it.” A native of Surfside Beach, Fry said he grew up in a “cinder block house with no heat or air conditioning.”
And he criticized several of his opponents without naming them. In a swipe at Graham, he said, “I didn’t inherit a record. I earned it.”
Lynch, owner of Jeff Lynch Appliance Center in Greenville, pointed to his business experience, saying he’s repeatedly grown the family business over the 40 years he’s been at the helm without going into debt.
“I understand budgets,” said Lynch, who came in a distant second to Graham in the June 9 GOP primary. “I know what being debt-free means. We can’t print money out of thin air in our business.”
Norman, a member of the hardline Freedom Caucus, also stressed his business credentials. A Rock Hill developer before entering politics, touted being “the most conservative.” He ended his pitch by declaring he’s “tired of moderates.”
Sanford talked about his record as governor and as the 1st District congressman.
Responding to a question about people living in the country illegally, he got a bit mixed up about his record.
He pointed to REAL ID as an example of results during his two terms as governor.
“We enacted it when I was governor,” he said. “A lot of governors weren’t doing it.”
Actually, in 2007, he signed a bill refusing to comply with the post-9/11 federal law to create a national ID standard. The Legislature reversed course in 2017, when it appeared enforcement would be imminent.
He meant to say E-Verify, a spokesman said after the debate. In 2008, Sanford signed legislation requiring businesses to use the E-Verify system to check workers’ legal status or else hire only people who hold a valid driver’s license from South Carolina or other state with similar license requirements. Three years later, then-Gov. Nikki Haley signed a law expanding on the requirements.

title: High stakes 2026 Michigan primary contests take center stage on Election Day
description: Hotly contested primaries across Michigan on Tuesday will shape the future of both major parties in the state. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. across most of Michigan. The exception is the four western Upper Peninsula counties bordering Wisconsin, where polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Central time. For […]
text:
iQoncept/Getty ImagesHotly contested primaries across Michigan on Tuesday will shape the future of both major parties in the state.
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. across most of Michigan. The exception is the four western Upper Peninsula counties bordering Wisconsin, where polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Central time.
For those who have not yet voted through absentee ballots or early voting opportunities, Tuesday is the last day Michiganders have to vote in the Aug. 4 primary.
Michigan Advance readers can view our 2026 Voter Guide for unbiased, essential information about each candidate in key races. 
Here are the top races across the Great Lakes State:
Democratic U.S. Senate primary — Haley Stevens vs. Abdul El-Sayed
The race between U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) and Abdul El-Sayed, former director of Wayne County’s Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services, has been one of the most watched U.S. Senate primary races in the nation. A battle of wills between the center-left establishment, represented by Stevens, and a surging progressive wave of young candidates, represented by El-Sayed, with the outcome potentially serving as a bellwether for progressive candidates in competitive states.
It could also reveal how purple of a state Michigan really is. Voters in the Great Lakes State last elected a Republican U.S. senator in 1994. However, the lone Republican in the race, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake, is endorsed by President Donald Trump and seen as the GOP’s best bet for beating the Democrats’ hold on the seat since 2001.
The choice between the two may also have implications in the national debate over which faction will assert control over the Democratic Party’s direction.
Check out Michigan Advance Senior Reporter Ben Solis’ deep dive into the race and the stakes at hand, gathered from more than a year on the campaign trail with El-Sayed and Stevens.

(Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Bernie Sanders, right, at a rally in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. The rally also included U.S. House candidate William Lawrence. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Republican gubernatorial primary — John James vs. Perry Johnson
Having started with a relatively crowded field — six candidates filed with the Michigan Bureau of Elections in the Republican primary — the race is now down to two: U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) and businessman Perry Johnson.
James and Johnson have been throwing campaign barbs and attacks at each other since Johnson entered the race at the start of 2026 — including a lawsuit Johnson filed in April that forced James to alter his campaign logo, as well as signature challenges traded between the two campaigns after the candidate filing deadline. 
Those attacks have only escalated as the primary approaches. Johnson has criticized James for taking campaign donations from both utility companies and data center developers, and has called him a liberal, tying him to U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids). 
James is hoping to glide to victory on name recognition, his endorsement by President Donald Trump and his record in Congress. Johnson, who has strong support from grassroots activists and spent most of his own money on the race, is aiming for a major political upset if he can beat James and move on to face the Democratic nominee in the fall.
Michigan Advance Reporter Katherine Dailey has been covering the ins and outs of the battle between James and Johnson, as well as the Democratic side of the race, which has all but been wrapped up by leading candidate and current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson. You can read Katherine’s deep dive into the race here.

John James delivers nominating petitions to the Michigan Bureau of Elections in Lansing in his bid for Republican nominee for governor. April 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Businessman Perry Johnson speaks with supporters and press prior to filing his signatures at the Michigan Bureau of Elections in Lansing. April 21, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. He was joined by former Michigan House Speaker Tom Leonard, right, who previously ran against James in the Republican primary for governor. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Republican candidate for governor Perry Johnson attends a rally calling for regulations on data centers on the Michigan Capitol steps. June 23, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceU.S. Rep. John James, R-Shelby Twp., speaks to reporters at the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's eighth and final State of the State address on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Democratic primaries in the 7th and 13th Congressional Districts
Much like the Democratic U.S. Senate race, the primary contests on Tuesday for the 7th and 13th Congressional Districts represent tests of whether progressive candidates can translate growing national enthusiasm into victories.
In the 7th District, representing Clinton, Ingham, Livingston and Shiawassee counties, most of Eaton County and parts of Genesee and Oakland counties, the seat is currently held by the Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett of Charlotte. Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink, former U.S. Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam and activist Will Lawrence are facing off to decide who will face Barrett in November.
Like El-Sayed, Lawrence is a progressive candidate who has campaigned by championing efforts to “guarantee healthcare for all” and enacting a federal moratorium on data centers. Brink and Maasdam have each tended to favor policies more toward the center. Brink seeks to extend and expand the Affordable Care Act, while Maasdam has said he wants to see data centers regulated on a local level.
Maasdam has been endorsed by U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) and also End Citizens United, a group that advocates for campaign finance reform and limiting the influence of money in politics. The senator’s endorsement holds serious sway — she represented the district before beating Rogers for the Senate seat she currently holds.
Brink has union backing — most prominently from the Michigan Education Association — and EMILYs List. She’s also been endorsed by former Michigan governors Jim Blanchard and Jennifer Granholm, and U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), adding a prominent progressive endorsement to her coalition.
Meanwhile, Michigan’s 13th Congressional District serves as a stronghold for Democrats and is made up of portions of Detroit, and its suburbs, including Allen Park, Hamtramck, Romulus and Wyandotte.
Currently held by U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar, the incumbent is being challenged by state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who represents the city in the state Legislature. McKinney is endorsed by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and El-Sayed, along with several other national progressives, including Detroit’s own U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib.
Thanedar does have support from key establishment Democrats, including U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and other party leaders, such as U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi).

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Meet the Gen Z journalist who bought his hometown newspaper in Georgia
description: Four years ago, Evan Newton was an intern at the Monticello News. Last month, he became the newspaper’s editor, publisher and owner after purchasing the outlet from its previous local owner.  At 25 years old, Newton is one of the youngest newspaper owners in Georgia. He told the Georgia Recorder that he got a “great […]
text:
Editor and owner of The Monticello News, Evan Newton, printed his first newspaper on July 22, 2026. Ellie Fivas/Georgia RecorderFour years ago, Evan Newton was an intern at the Monticello News. Last month, he became the newspaper’s editor, publisher and owner after purchasing the outlet from its previous local owner. 
At 25 years old, Newton is one of the youngest newspaper owners in Georgia. He told the Georgia Recorder that he got a “great deal” on the sale because Katherine Mudd, the paper’s previous owner, wanted to keep ownership local. If Newton hadn’t agreed to purchase the newspaper, Mudd said a corporate buyer would have likely been her next option.
While Newton didn’t share the value of the sale, he said he dipped into his savings for the purchase and is even considering buying more local newsrooms in the future. 
Newton’s purchase not only gained local and statewide attention, but also national buzz. He said all kinds of people have offered their congratulations and thanks to him for still believing enough in community journalism to purchase his hometown newspaper, which covers Jasper County – home to about 18,000 people – in central Georgia. 
“The response has been overwhelmingly positive,” Newton said. “It really just has me fired up to keep pushing this paper in the right direction and really make something that our community can be proud of.”
A sign that Gen Z believes in future of local journalism? 
Local journalism is often described as being in “crisis.” On average, nonprofit Rebuild Local News estimates 2.5 local newsrooms shut down per week, creating news deserts — places where no newsrooms report on local issues. 
About 5 million Georgians lack access to local reporting, making it the worst state for news deserts in the country, according to research from Northwestern University.
It’s not necessarily a secure time to purchase a local newspaper. According to the Pew Research Center, 39% of Americans say their local newspaper is not doing well financially. But Newton was optimistic about the future of his new business. 
“I knew that I had an opportunity to not sit on the sidelines, but to really do something about the state of local journalism,” Newton said. 
Amanda Bright, who is a University of Georgia clinical associate professor and who leads the Cox Institute Journalism Innovation Lab, said she was thrilled to hear about the newspaper’s sale. 
“All the positive philanthropic things that we have seen over the last few years — people trying to support and help grow local news — is fine and all,” said Bright, who has worked with the Monticello News in the past. “But it was never going to be sustainable unless the next generation said local news matters.”
Bright said that’s exactly what has happened with Newton and the Monticello News. She said Generation Z has increasingly shown more interest in local news, which, in her view, will be the reason that the industry survives the decline of print journalism. According to Bright, over 200 programs nationwide allow students to embed themselves in local newsrooms, which allows them to understand the value of community journalism. 
Bright said Newton is just one example of how many “mission-driven” young people are investing in local journalism, despite the pressures of the industry today.  
A photo of the original Monticello News building from the 1860s in their downtown office. Ellie Fivas/Georgia Recorder
“There is a trend, and I’m seeing it among my students as they go out into the industry, of them feeling called to do this work,” she said. “He’s definitely not alone in trying to do this, and I think that’s even more exciting.”
Newton said he believes the key to surviving the decline of local news is a combination of the old and the new. Older readers can still count on finding print copies of the Monticello News on their grocery store newsstands — because Newton knows older generations still value that form of journalism. But Newton said he is also excited for the paper’s digital future: curating a strong social media presence, focusing on digital advertising and even releasing a podcast someday. 
Instead of wholly reinventing the Monticello News, Newton said he hopes to meet readers where they are, from print newspaper loyalists to his own chronically online generation. 
“Local papers need to adapt to avoid falling behind, and that’s what we’re trying to do now,” he said. “This may be because I work in it, but I’ve never been under the impression that local journalism is going to die.”
Meet the reporter, editor, publisher and owner
Newton will be the only full-time staff member of the Monticello News, aided by two part-time staff members, community contributors and an intern. Within a week, he gained the responsibility of being the paper’s editor, publisher and owner. The first printed edition under his ownership included a layout redesign and several local news stories — nearly all written by Newton.
Newton knows he’s under pressure to deliver a great product to his community. But he said he feels more at ease running the Monticello News than in any of his other positions because his readers are his friends and neighbors. 
Newton shared that he had been approached previously about purchasing the newspaper but had declined. This time, though, he said he felt ready to take on the responsibility of running his hometown outlet — a newspaper he first fell in love with while reading the crime reports and local sports section as a kid. 
Newton said he’s looking forward to doing more “fearless journalism” and looks forward to covering issues like data center development and local government scandals. 
Today, people have 24/7 access to worldwide news, but Newton said local news fills a niche that readers still need, covering regional governments, community events and local culture. 
Evan Newton, a 25-year-old from Monticello, purchased his hometown newspaper after interning there only 3 years before. Ellie Fivas/Georgia Recorder
“Just because it’s ‘boring’ doesn’t mean it isn’t necessary,” he said. “If you don’t have local papers that are covering things, it will lead to an uninformed and uneducated community … I know what we’re doing is both a service but also just necessary for the everyday ins and outs of the community.”
During the Georgia Recorder’s interview with Newton, a woman walked into his office — an old brick building that’s housed the newspaper since the early 1900s. Newton stood and met the woman at the front desk for a long-winded explanation of her advertising problem. 
Despite being only a week into ownership, Newton listened carefully, admitting he’s new to the job and fixed the issue as best he could. Later he said an owner with roots in Monticello can make better connections with the community than a corporate owner. 
He noted that few community newsrooms still remain under local ownership. When 70-year-old Mudd decided to retire, Newton said he knew it was time to return home to Monticello and do his part to save local journalism.
“This is the place that I have always called home,” Newton said. “No matter how hard you try, it’s the people living and working in the community that can best tell the story of Jasper County.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: More than 1 million Ohioans aren’t getting essential safety-net benefits, analysis shows
description: More than 1 million Ohioans are not getting essential safety-net benefits for which they’re eligible, according to a new analysis by the Urban Institute. In many cases, just a fraction of low-income families are getting help with things such as energy assistance. As electricity and grocery bills continue to spike, low-income families’ need for such […]
text:
The entrance to a Big Lots store in Portland, Oregon. (Stock photo by hapabapa/Getty Images)More than 1 million Ohioans are not getting essential safety-net benefits for which they’re eligible, according to a new analysis by the Urban Institute. In many cases, just a fraction of low-income families are getting help with things such as energy assistance.
As electricity and grocery bills continue to spike, low-income families’ need for such benefits seems likely to intensify. But why they might be eligible and still not get them isn’t as straightforward.
“Eligibility depends on national and state eligibility policies and the demographic and income characteristics of the population,” the Urban Institute said in its State of the Safety Net report, which was published last week. 
“Participation rates among those eligible for a program depend on many factors, including funding levels, administrative procedures, awareness of programs and their policies, and the decisions made by individuals in the context of their family situations.”
In other words, some eligible people might not be taking advantage of the programs because they can’t or don’t want to. But many others might not know about them, there might not be enough money to provide benefits to all who are eligible, or the paperwork hassle is too much to overcome, the analysis said.
In any case, millions are not getting help in Ohio who theoretically could, it showed.
For example, in 2023 just 1 in 5 of the 1.4 million households eligible for the Low Income Energy Assistance Program participated.
That compares to one-third in Pennsylvania, 20% in West Virginia, one-fourth in Kentucky, 17% in Indiana, and two-thirds in Michigan.
Energy assistance is critical to vulnerable populations. Policy Matters Ohio reports that in the Buckeye State, nearly half — 46.5% — of households receiving assistance in 2023 included a person with a disability. In addition, 39.5% had at least one person 60 or older and 14% had a child under 6.
Research has shown that states that administer block grants for things like energy assistance through active outreach have higher participation rates than those that simply wait for people to apply.
There were smaller variations in federal housing assistance. In 2023 in Ohio, 30.2% of 653,000 eligible households received it. That compares to 29.4% in Pennsylvania, 36.7% in West Virginia, 31.9% in Kentucky, 25.7% in Indiana, and 28.6% in Michigan.
Perhaps explaining the greater consistency, the Urban Institute report said the housing program is underfunded, so the available funding might be exhausted by providing benefits to similar shares of states’ eligible populations.
Also serving just a fraction of those eligible is Temporary Assistance to Needy Families. 
It’s cash assistance to those with very low incomes. To qualify in 2023, a family of three must have made less than $12,432 that year. 
In Ohio, just over a fifth of the 190,000 eligible families received benefits in 2023. In Pennsylvania, 17.8% did. In West Virginia, just 15.1% did, followed by 14.7% in Kentucky, 8.5% in Michigan, and just 5.9% in Indiana.
In a 2023 report, the Urban Institute said participation rates in the program have plummeted since it was converted into a block grant in 1996. 
Often to control growth in the cost of safety-net programs, the federal government converted some into block grants and gave states much control over how to administer them.
In 2023, 57.2% of the 2.3 million Ohioans eligible for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program received benefits. In Pennsylvania, 59.9% did. In West Virginia, it was 49.9%. In Kentucky, it was 55.2%. In Indiana, 59.2% and in Michigan 56.3%,
That means millions of eligible people in those and other states aren’t getting modest nutrition assistance as food costs continue to rise.
Many more are likely to lose help. 
President Donald Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill that was passed last summer made the deepest cuts in the history of the program — $186 billion over 10 years.

title: It was supposed to be a haven for troubled teens. They risked everything to escape.
authors: Brittany Hailer, The Marshall Project, Ilica Mahajan, The Marshall Project
description: Additional reporting by Rachel Dissell This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook. ST. CLAIRSVILLE, OHIO – Paitin Pahoundis jolted awake, a siren blaring in her ears. Her friend Saman[...]
text:
Clockwise from top left: Paitin Pahoundis, who spent time at the Fox Run Center for Children and Adolescents; a view of the Fox Run facility; Isabella Ramirez, who also spent time at Fox Run; and a view of the sign for Fox Run. (Photos by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)Additional reporting by Rachel Dissell
This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.
ST. CLAIRSVILLE, OHIO – Paitin Pahoundis jolted awake, a siren blaring in her ears. Her friend Samantha Primeau was in her room. It was time. The other girls, Samantha told her, were gone. They had jammed a sprinkler, triggering the fire alarm and filling the hallway outside with water.
Their escape plan was working. But there was a problem: Paitin didn’t have shoes.
The checkered Vans and the white Jordans with the bright orange stripes that her father had bought her before he went to prison, the ones she meticulously kept in mint condition, had been taken by staff and locked in another room, along with the rest of her possessions. She was on “no personals” status for not following the rules.
But, Paitin wanted out, and this was her chance.
As they walked out of the building and into a snowstorm, Paitin remembers a staff member standing in a doorway. She looked at Paitin and said, “If you want to go, just go.”
Over the five years reviewed, law enforcement officials visited the Fox Run facility, on average, once every 21 days. They went for 52 assaults and 17 sexual assaults. (Photo by Nate Smallwood for The Marshall Project.)
Both teens said they dreamed of escaping the staff members who forcibly held them down hard enough to leave bruises, the blood in the hallways from kids cutting themselves, the girls strangling themselves with bedsheets, the adults who insisted no family wanted to adopt them and who looked through them like they were already gone.
On that January night in 2022, the girls careened down the hill below the Fox Run Center for Children and Adolescents, their pumping adrenaline temporarily masking the frigid Ohio air. Not even Paitin’s soaking wet socks slipping off in the snow could deter her descent toward freedom.
Barefoot, Paitin crossed the highway that snakes along the back end of Fox Run’s grounds, dodging cars and climbing over medians. As they considered going to a nearby hotel, things started to fall apart.
Electric pain ripped through Paitin’s frozen feet. Samantha felt herself getting sleepy and slowed to a crawl, wishing she could pass out right there. They had nowhere to go. All they could do was turn back in failure.
At the top of the hill, police dragged Paitin into a squad car. She pounded the window, screaming in agony. Before she was hospitalized, Paitin recalls a staff member walking up and peering in. “I bet you will never do that again, will you?”
She would, she told herself. “I would rather be dead outside in the snow.”
Samantha Primeau spent time in and out of residential treatment centers as a teenager. She escaped together with Paitin Pahoundis from the Fox Run Center for Children and Adolescents during a snowstorm in January of 2022. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
Paitin and Samantha desperately wanted to escape what was supposed to be a therapeutic haven for kids with mental health and behavioral issues. Instead, they found themselves confined for months — in Paitin’s case, years — inside an institution where they witnessed kids routinely attacking and sexually assaulting each other, anarchic riots by children pushed to the breaking point, and suicide attempts using makeshift weapons fashioned from scraps of metal or bedsheets, according to police and state records and numerous interviews.
They endured violence from some of the adults charged with their care, medically unnecessary sedative injections and long, painful periods of being physically held down by staff. Many of those same episodes, some of which ended with children in handcuffs or ambulances, appear to be missing from the state’s own oversight records, according to an analysis by The Marshall Project. This leaves parents, caseworkers, regulators, and the judges deciding where to place kids in foster care with an incomplete picture of what was happening behind the facility’s locked doors.
Paitin spent three years at Fox Run in St. Clairsville, Ohio. She escaped multiple times and once made it across the state line from Ohio into West Virginia in an attempt. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
Did you experience abuse or trauma in a youth residential treatment center? Did you work at a youth residential treatment center? We want to hear your story.
As the number of youth prisons dwindles in a nationwide push for rehabilitation over punishment, the juvenile justice system continues to place kids in residential treatment facilities like Fox Run. However, advocates say the facilities are “virtually indistinguishable from incarceration.” Some, like one in Pennsylvania with a record of child abuse, have secured contracts to house migrant children amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Fox Run, one of Ohio’s largest youth residential treatment centers, is owned by Universal Health Services, a Pennsylvania-based Fortune 500 company. It’s a privately operated, 100-bed facility housing boys and girls as young as 5 from as far away as Alaska. Many of the youth are sent by their parents, foster care agencies, and juvenile courts. County governments across Ohio have paid Fox Run millions of dollars to house children who have complex mental health or behavioral needs, according to county contracts.
Kids were sent to Fox Run following suicide attempts or fights while in foster care. Others were placed by their parents at a doctor’s recommendation after a suicide attempt. Some, like Paitin, who lived at the facility for three years, found themselves at Fox Run because no foster parent would take them.
To understand what was happening inside Fox Run, The Marshall Project reviewed hundreds of pages of police and state inspection reports between 2020 and 2025, obtained through public records requests, and interviewed seven women previously housed in the facility. These records and interviews told stories of children desperate to escape, fleeing into cornfields, sprinting into traffic, and attempting to hitchhike. Former Fox Run staff members said the youth turned violent inside the facility because they were pushed to their limit. Many eventually ended up in juvenile detention as their behavior escalated. They thought ending up behind bars, like facing the frozen woods, would be an improvement over Fox Run.
In a statement, Fox Run CEO Randy MacKendrick said the facility serves children with “complex behavioral health needs” and that incidents involving aggression, self-harm, suicide and attempts to leave the facility are “unfortunately not uncommon among this high-acuity population.”
“Fox Run cooperates with state regulators and other oversight agencies, investigates concerns, and implements corrective actions whenever warranted,” MacKendrick added. “When concerns arise, they are reviewed promptly and, when appropriate, reported to the appropriate regulatory and law enforcement authorities.”
While officials from the Belmont County Sheriff’s Office diligently documented desperate attempts by children to get out of Fox Run, often through violence, many of those incidents were absent from a database maintained by the Department of Behavioral Health, the state agency charged with licensing and inspecting the facility. The Ohio Department of Behavioral Health and Belmont County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
 What They’re Running From

Two years after Paitin and Samantha briefly considered seeking help at the nearby hotel, a 12-year-old trans boy walked into its lobby.
He fled Fox Run after a girl entered his room while he was sleeping, pressed a pillow over his head and wrapped her hands around his neck, according to a sheriff’s office report. Another youth stole a staff member’s keys and let the boy out.
He ran down the hill, crossed the highway and reached the hotel, where he told workers he was a runaway. They called the police. He was returned to Fox Run and arrested for theft. He had taken the keys with him when he fled.
Over the five years of police records reviewed by The Marshall Project, law enforcement officials visited the facility, on average, once every 21 days. They went for 52 assaults and 17 sexual assaults; some of those cases involved allegations of physical and sexual violence by staff. Police also responded to calls for unruly behavior or kids running away, or went to the facility after family members called for wellness checks because they couldn’t reach their children, or because their children reported abuses.
In March 2022, a staff member reported to police that an 11-year-old “forcibly sodomized” a 9-year-old boy while several other youths barricaded the door with a mattress. A Fox Run nurse told a detective that understaffing meant staff frequently left the floor “leaving the juveniles unattended.” Others said workers might have been out on smoke breaks.
The child was initially taken to a nearby hospital, but the facility lacked anyone certified to conduct a forensic examination. A nurse ordered a transfer to a hospital with trained personnel, but the child was instead returned to Fox Run without receiving a forensic exam.
The next day, when the nurse realized the child had missed the appointment, she contacted the police, reporting significant bruising to the face and rectal area. She said Fox Run staff delayed the child’s exam while waiting for permission from an out-of-state guardian and expressed serious concern for the child’s well-being, according to a sheriff’s office report.
When an officer returned to Fox Run, they found staff members were unclear on procedures for handling sexual assault allegations. It was only when the officer ultimately contacted the child’s out-of-state caseworker for verbal consent that the process of securing the necessary exam moved forward — a day later than the nurse’s order.
Two years later, state inspectors found Fox Run mishandled a separate sexual misconduct complaint — with staff encouraging a girl to work on her “assertiveness skills” after a male resident exposed himself and touched her, instead of addressing the boy’s actions.
Police also documented cases of staff directly causing harm to children.
In 2022, a staff member “violently” kicked an 11-year-old and after she was fired, she admitted to police that “she had done wrong.” She pleaded guilty to assault and was sentenced to 180 days in jail. In 2024, another staffer was terminated when he shoved his elbow into a boy’s mouth, leaving a visible red mark, after the boy hit him with a broom and called him a racial obscenity.
Last year, state inspectors discovered a child with a chipped tooth was not taken to a dentist for more than two months, nor were they given their prescribed antibiotics. Fox Run management subsequently reported a staff nurse to the state nursing board over the incident. State records indicate several suspected abuse cases in which MacKendrick, or another manager, personally called police, fired employees or notified other authorities.
Abigail, who was placed at Fox Run in late 2020 after a suicide attempt and asked to be identified only by her first name, remembers hearing other girls, including Paitin, screaming while being physically restrained by staff.
Legally, residential treatment staff can physically restrain a child by holding them to stop them from moving, typically because they believe the child is a danger to themselves or others. Sometimes staff will hold kids on the ground, against a wall or bend them over from behind. The use of mechanical devices — like belts, straps or harnesses — to restrain anyone under the age of 18 is prohibited in the state of Ohio and The Marshall Project’s review of state oversight reports and police records did not uncover evidence of these kinds of mechanical restraints being used.
“You just hear [her] screaming like, ‘I can’t breathe. You’re hurting me,’” Abigail said. “You’re listening to this, and there’s nothing anybody can do, and we’re all just like, in the room. I was sobbing. There were a lot of other people crying. People are trying to comfort other people … You’re just exposed constantly to violence from staff, violence from kids.”
Isabella Ramirez, who also lived in Fox Run with Paitin, said that kids would regularly misbehave in the hopes of being sent to juvenile detention. “At Fox Run, we begged the officers. We’d be bad in front of the officers just so they’d take us.” Isabella, who also had traumatizing experiences at several other residential treatment centers throughout her teens, recalled. “But they couldn’t take no more because the cells were full.”
Isabella Ramirez, who also lived in Fox Run, said that kids would regularly misbehave in the hopes of being sent to juvenile detention. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
Recalling when she was held down by Fox Run workers, Isabella said, “[My skin] was purple. And I could get gasps of air out, saying I could not breathe.” Memories of the younger children at Fox Run, ages 5 to 6, who were held in what she said was called the “Dreams Unit,” still haunt her.
“Grown men would throw them like ragdolls,” she said of the children. “They’re just so little. They’re scared.”
Last July, a 15-year-old girl told a staff member, “I will do whatever I can to get the fuck out of this place,” after using metal brackets from the ceiling to cut her arm and threatening to cut staff members, according to a sheriff’s office report.
In 2021, a teenager who was denied the use of crutches by Fox Run staff, “immediately begged not to be taken back to the facility” after a police officer called for an ambulance to treat her injured leg and self-harm injuries.
If you spent time in a youth residential treatment center, you are legally entitled to request official records about what happened to you. Read our guide showing how to get them.

Fox Run reported 126 suicide attempts to state inspectors from January 2022 to June 2025, a number that Marissa C. Nardi, lead counsel at youth advocacy nonprofit Children’s Rights, said “is not normal” and should “deeply alarm the state and prompt a thorough investigation.”
Children who attempted suicide at Fox Run sometimes found themselves behind bars with criminal charges because they threatened or attacked staff after wrapping bedsheets around their necks, cutting themselves or trying to swallow screws.
“If kids locked in a treatment facility are being traumatized instead of treated, to the point of regularly attempting suicide, fleeing into the woods, or seeking incarceration as a safer option, there is no acceptable justification for the state to keep placing children there,” Nardi said.
Using detention as a response to youth acting out in distress is a system failure, said Jeffrey Shook, a professor of social work, law and sociology at the University of Pittsburgh. Once children are in these systems, behavior gets criminalized, leading to deeper justice involvement rather than meaningful help. Mobile crisis teams or outside social workers, he said, should respond to calls involving youth crises while in psychiatric care.
“Taking that sheet and attempting to hang yourself. You’re saying something right there,” Shook said. ”Are we listening to that?”
 An Industry Under Scrutiny

Since the 1950s, youth residential treatment centers, often rooted in religious-based behavior modification methods, have evolved into substance use or mental health treatment centers, boarding schools or wilderness camps. (Fox Run and its parent company are not religiously affiliated). The industry remains loosely regulated due to weak federal oversight and insufficient tracking of abuses, experts say.
The number of youth involved in the juvenile justice system who were placed in residential treatment facilities was around 29,300 in 2023, a jump of 4,400 from just two years earlier, figures from the Department of Justice show. At the beginning of this year, roughly 1,000 children were living in around 140 facilities in Ohio, according to state data.
Universal Health Services has faced two federal probes into its care of children, including one that led to a $122 million settlement with the federal government in 2020 after allegations that the company billed taxpayers for medically unnecessary services while failing to provide adequate care to patients. UHS was also the subject of a $553 million verdict in a negligence lawsuit in 2024, which the company settled out of court last year.
Fox Run’s parent company, Universal Health Services, has faced two federal probes into its care of children. (Photo by Nate Smallwood for The Marshall Project.)
The U.S. Senate Finance Committee investigated UHS in 2024, alongside three other residential treatment providers. The committee found evidence of systemic abuse in different facilities across the four companies.
The committee’s report included two UHS facilities in Ohio — Belmont Pines Hospital in Youngstown and Foundations for Living in Mansfield — where records documented children being assaulted, improperly restrained and inappropriately medicated. Routine inspections by Ohio regulators have documented similar conditions at Fox Run.
In a response to the committee’s 2024 report, the company called the findings “incomplete and misleading.” UHS maintained that it took action when appropriate and thoroughly investigated allegations made by individuals and inspectors.
The Senate report “fails to recognize the thousands of children helped by our facilities over the years; children whose lives have been greatly enhanced as a result of their stay and the treatment they received,” UHS’ response read.
The conditions at residential facilities have even attracted celebrity attention. In 2024, Paris Hilton testified before Congress that she experienced physical and sexual abuse as a teenager at a residential treatment center in Utah and has pushed for reform.
Even so, a 2024 report from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General found that nearly a third of states cannot identify patterns of maltreatment in residential facilities because they do not consistently track where abuse occurs.
Enough people have been traumatized by going through the system that a community on Reddit for “survivors and advocates who oppose the abusive Troubled Teen Industry” has swelled to tens of thousands of users over the past 15 years.
Organizations like Breaking Code Silence and Unsilenced gather testimony from people who experienced mistreatment. They also collect government documents — including inspections, investigations and citations of facilities across the country. Each website also offers templates and instructions for former residents to request their records from facilities.
 ‘No Child Should Be in There’

Six months before her escape in the snow, Paitin ran away with her friend Isabella. They were a part of a group of 10 girls, one of whom was hospitalized after she threatened to run into traffic. They made it about 10 miles down the road to Wheeling, West Virginia.
Police picked them up after the pair contacted their parents, who turned them in. The girls told Fox Run staff they’d hitchhiked with a local man who bought them clothes at Target and gave them money. Isabella said the man had a brother who had been placed in Fox Run. He understood their desire for freedom.
In bodycam footage obtained by The Marshall Project, an officer searching for the girls expresses his frustration on a phone call. “That fucking place needs [to be] shut down. I’m tired of it … I said this is ridiculous … Fucking shit hole,” the officer says.
“They’re just going to run again later,” he added, referring to the girls.
In a still from an officer’s bodycam footage, she and another sheriff’s officer searched a thick field of flowers for Paitin and Bella after an escape attempt. (Source: Belmont Sheriff’s Office.)
Several other adults connected to Fox Run shared the officer’s frustrations. In interviews, five former Fox Run employees told The Marshall Project that children lived in a constant state of crisis. One worker, Julie Lipscomb, was left with bruises, nerve damage from a bite wound and stress so severe she said her hair began falling out. “That place could turn the nicest person into what they feel like is a monster,” she said.
Sydney Smith, who worked at Fox Run for about four months last year after graduating high school nearby, underwent training on physically restraining kids before stepping out on the floor at Fox Run. But she said she wasn’t prepared for the reality of what she was asked to do.
“You were pinning children to the floor, usually one person on each arm and a person like laying perpendicular over their body,” Smith said. “And then somebody holding their head where they couldn’t bite you.”
State inspectors cited Fox Run multiple times for its use of restraints, inspection records show. One child under age 9 was held down for a full hour, double the state’s maximum time limit. Four other children were restrained for “substantial” periods despite being described as “calm, non-combative and quiet.” In 2022, inspectors found Fox Run injected children with sedatives without a clear link to a psychiatric condition.
Wendy Opic, who worked at Fox Run when Isabella and Paitin were there, said she still prays for the children inside the facility. She remembers a manager thanking her for de-escalating children through conversation instead of restraining them. “Isn’t this what you’re supposed to do?” Opic thought to herself. “Be nice to these children?”
“I kept thinking, how do you get this place shut down? Because I don’t know how to do anything like that. No child should be in there,” she said.
As she cried, she added: “They were just treated like animals.”
Wendy Opic, a former Fox Run employee, said she still prays for the children inside the facility. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
 What Regulators Can’t See

The Marshall Project obtained inspection reports from the Department of Behavioral Health — the state agency regulating residential facilities for kids with significant behavioral health needs, like Fox Run — from September 2021 to February 2025. Inspectors cited Fox Run for unsafe restraints, medical neglect, understaffing and deteriorating facility conditions. However, inspection records do not show state follow-up investigations tied to those incidents.
Additionally, it seems that many incidents may have never reached regulators’ attention. An analysis of Fox Run’s self-reported incident data from January 2022 through June of 2025 found that at least 40 incidents involving police did not appear in state documents. An Ohio statute requires residential treatment facilities to report suicide attempts, arrests, assaults and child hospitalizations to the state within 24 hours of the occurrence.
The incidents for which the state had no record included: a child being arrested or taken to a juvenile detention center (21 incidents), assaults (15 incidents), and hospitalizations or evaluations by emergency medical services (9 incidents). The story of the trans boy who was arrested after being assaulted and escaping to the hotel did not appear in these official records.
The Department of Behavioral Health did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Paitin desperately wanted to escape what was supposed to be a therapeutic haven for kids. Instead, she found herself routinely witnessing kids attacking and sexually assaulting each other. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
Of the 40 incidents that did not appear in state records, MacKendrick, the Fox Run CEO, said that a state review showed that some “were not reportable” while others “were appropriately reported,” but did not indicate which, or how many, of the dozens of incidents fell into each category.
MacKendrick noted that the facility had not been cited for violating the law for its handling of the reporting of any of the incidents The Marshall Project identified as not being in the state’s database.
Lax government oversight has largely been the norm for Ohio’s youth residential treatment industry. While several of the state’s residential treatment centers have voluntarily surrendered their licenses to operate following pressure from media or investigative agencies, only a few have actually had their licenses revoked. Most companies instead reach settlements with the state.
A watchdog group, Disability Rights Ohio, has the right under the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 to investigate residential treatment facilities, usually triggered by complaints from children and parents. The group’s investigations in recent years led to voluntary license suspensions by Sequel Pomegranate Health Systems in Columbus and Youth Intensive Services in Youngstown.
However, some state lawmakers want to force regulators into more aggressive responses when facilities harm children. A bill recently introduced in the Ohio House of Representatives by Rep. Crystal Lett would require the Department of Behavioral Health to take measures against youth treatment facilities with incidents of violence and other serious violations. That could mean even shutting them down rather than leaving the agency with discretion over what sanctions to impose, if any.
Lett said she introduced the measure in response to The Marshall Project’s investigation in November 2025 that revealed escalating violence, staff injuries and campus-wide fights at Mohican Young Star Academy, Ohio’s largest youth treatment facility. The report also led to the state suspending admissions to the facility and a license revocation hearing that began this June.
“With respect to the revocation hearing, we are unable to comment on pending litigation. We look forward to vindicating our rights through the appropriate legal process and do not believe there is merit to the alleged violations,” Mohican owner Zach Logan wrote in an email.
Isabella, who is raising her toddler, has been accepted to college. She wants to go into nursing to help kids like her. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
Mohican, which rebranded as Empowering to Elevate Academy in late 2025, has previously withstood at least two state efforts to shut it down. In 2021, former Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost sued to remove the facility’s then-operator, Olga Strasser, over allegations of improper restraints, but a judge dismissed the case for lack of evidence. Yost vowed to move forward with revoking the facility’s license, but the state’s ongoing effort hasn’t been successful.
“Just the fact that it’s continuing in real time. It was our proof that this isn’t a hypothetical situation that we’re legislating for. It’s a real situation unfolding,” Lett said in April of this year. “I can’t help thinking: If my kid were in there right now, what am I doing to help that kid?”
For the children who have come out the other side of living in residential treatment, the healing process is often a slow one.
Years after her escape and discharge, Paitin still has the shoes staff members took from her, but she never put them on after getting out. She’s kept them pristine, a cherished object from her dad. “It hurts me to see them dirty,” she said. When he visited her at her new apartment, he immediately noticed the shoes. “He looked happy,” Paitin said.
Paitin, Samantha and Isabella have a collection of various items from their stays in Fox Run and other residential treatment facilities: clothes with their initials still written on the tags, journals, drawings, and, for some of them, medical records detailing psychiatric treatment.
When Paitin requested her records, Fox Run administrators told her she’d have to return to the facility to get her paper documents. She said she had a panic attack in the parking lot and couldn’t set foot in the building.
It’s just one way the facility’s impact lingers.
“I did a lot of crazy things in residential, but it was because of the environment. There’s only so much a person can take,” said Samantha, who now spends as much time as she can in nature, reading and taking photos with friends. (Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project.)
“I’m more quiet, reserved now, and it’s just not who I remember me being,” Paitin said. “Like, it makes me want to cry. I remember being so bubbly and everything. Now I just feel like I’m stuck in the same mindset … It’s kind of like I’m numb.”
She still dreams of running. Sometimes she wakes up and forgets she’s no longer locked inside Fox Run. Other days, she dreams of what life is like outside of Ohio and its expanse of cornfields. For now, she leans on her friends. They Snapchat, call and text each other. They gather evidence and give it to a journalist. They hope for change.
“I just feel bad for the kids that are still there,” Paitin said.

title: Ohio should treat the threat of radioactive fracking waste like the emergency that it is
description: Southeastern Ohio has a serious problem underground. Now that problem is reaching the surface and threatening our drinking water.  As a petroleum geologist, my job is to understand the rock layers deep underground and how fluids move through them. In Washington County, Ohio, toxic, radioactive waste from failed fracking waste disposal wells is surfacing wher[...]
text:
Workers in Ohio unload hydraulic fracking fluids from a tank truck at an injection well, where the toxic waste will be pumped deep underground. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images.)Southeastern Ohio has a serious problem underground. Now that problem is reaching the surface and threatening our drinking water. 
As a petroleum geologist, my job is to understand the rock layers deep underground and how fluids move through them. 
In Washington County, Ohio, toxic, radioactive waste from failed fracking waste disposal wells is surfacing where it should never be — near homes, farms, natural gas wells, streams, and schools. State leaders need to treat this like the emergency it is.
Fracking wastewater is not ordinary water. It carries heavy metals, toxic chemicals, and radioactive material — not things that people, animals, plants, or waterways should be exposed to. 
Safely injecting it underground requires rock that is deep, porous, and sealed off from drinking water and the surface. This means a reservoir with room for the waste, a trap to keep it enclosed, and a seal that ensures it cannot escape. 
In Washington County, those basic conditions do not appear to exist, and the consequences are now measurable. 
The evidence indicates there are fractures allowing the injected wastewater to flow up into shallower layers and to the surface. 
What’s unfolding in Southeastern Ohio is a manmade geological disaster, and it is getting worse.
A graphic provided by Marietta College petroleum geologist David Jeffery shows how fracking injection wells fail to keep waste contained.
The evidence: rising pressure and invaded wells
The clearest warning sign is pressure. Fluids underground flow from high pressure towards low pressure. 
Gas wells producing from a shallower layer, the Berea Sandstone, have seen pressures climb from roughly 50 pounds per square inch (psi) to more than 350 psi in under a year, to the point where they are in danger of blowing out. 
That is a dangerous signal. Producing gas wells lose pressure over time as they deplete — they don’t gain it. The rising pressures mean something is pushing fluid into these layers.
Tests indicate that that something is fracking wastewater. It has infiltrated more than 100 gas wells in the area, some over five miles from the disposal wells themselves, destroying gas production and the livelihoods of the well operators — our neighbors and friends — who depend on it.
This toxic waste also threatens our drinking water sources.
Two things the state must do now:
First, take control of the pressure. The state needs to take over both the injection wells and the invaded gas wells and begin actively drawing fluids out. 
Pulling pressure down creates a low-pressure sink that draws contaminated fluid back away from the surrounding aquifers and producing wells, stranding it before it can migrate further. 
Once the spread is under control, the dozens of well operators and landowners who have already lost their livelihoods will need to be compensated.
Second, protect the drinking water. This is the piece that should alarm everyone, because it isn’t a local problem — it’s a regional one. 
The migrating waste threatens the freshwater aquifers supplying drinking water to more than a dozen communities: Beverly, Lowell, Devola, Marietta, Belpre, Little Hocking, Coolville, and Cutler, Ohio, along with Williamstown, Boaz, Vienna, Parkersburg, Blennerhassett, and Lubeck, West Virginia. 
That’s more than a hundred thousand people whose water supply stands to be impacted by this problem.
A first step, but not enough
Recently, the Ohio Department of Natural Resources finally acted, requesting voluntary suspension of operations at four injection wells. 
After months — arguably years — of inaction in the face of residents begging for help on the issue, that acknowledgment matters. 
But “voluntary” and “four wells” are not proportional to a problem spreading across a region. 
There seems to be an inability to face the fact that there is a catastrophic escape of the waste — indicating a total failure of the fracking waste injection program. 
The governor should declare a state of emergency in the impacted part of Washington County.
The cost of waiting
This will cost money. Waiting will cost far more. 
If radioactive brine reaches the drinking-water aquifers, cleanup costs could jump from millions of dollars to hundreds of millions — or billions. 
Families, farmers, small operators, and entire towns would pay for a failure they didn’t cause.
Communities across the region are united on this because the stakes are simple — clean water, safe homes, and honest government. 
Ohioans should be able to trust that state agencies will act when the facts are in front of them.
Washington County is sounding the alarm. Columbus needs to listen — before our drinking water is tainted by toxic waste.
Stop the injection. Lower the pressure. Protect the aquifers. Do it now.
