name: Daily Montanan
title: Smoke clears for parts of Montana, though may be short-lived
description: While two-thirds of Montana is getting a bit of relief from wildfire smoke, conditions in the western portion likely will continue to be smoky, according to the Montana Department of Environmental Quality. By Monday afternoon, smoke had cleared out of much of the central portion of the state, with Great Falls, Helena and Havre all […]
text:
Helicopter on Skillet Fire on July 31st, 2026. (Photo via Inciweb, Skillet Fire)While two-thirds of Montana is getting a bit of relief from wildfire smoke, conditions in the western portion likely will continue to be smoky, according to the Montana Department of Environmental Quality.
By Monday afternoon, smoke had cleared out of much of the central portion of the state, with Great Falls, Helena and Havre all seeing clear air. Billings, Bozeman and Butte were still dealing with moderate air quality impacts on Monday, as were Glendive and Glasgow.
Missoula and much of the Bitterroot and Flathead valleys were dealing with significant smoke impacts, with air quality scores reaching toward and above 200 in “unhealthy” or into the red, on Sunday night.
“Behind a cool front, a northerly flow will keep much of the heavy smoke out of central, northern, and eastern Montana on Monday,” a Monday DEQ smoke update said. “However, the same cannot be said for the western third of the state, where heavy smoke will remain a concern.”
Temperatures are also expected to begin a climb back up after a brief reprieve for the state on Sunday and Monday.
Lincoln, Flathead, Lake, Sanders, Mineral, Ravalli, Missoula, Beaverhead, Deer Lodge, Granite, and Silver Bow Counties were under an air quality alert on Monday into Tuesday.
According to the DEQ, those alerts are issued when the 24-hour cumulative air quality gets into the unhealthy for sensitive groups category, or when 24-hour cumulative air quality is likely to move into that part of the air quality scale.
Matt Ludwig, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Great Falls said they were keeping an eye on temperatures and humidity — both important parts of fire weather — for Friday and Saturday.
Much of the state was under a red-flag warning throughout the weekend, which means that a variety of factors have combined to make dangerous fire conditions more likely.
“We’re keeping an eye on the possibility of these low humidity conditions plus maybe some increased wind speeds, so we’re at least looking at an elevated chance for fire weather conditions through most of the week,” Ludwig said.
Smoke from regional wildfires, including intense blazes in and around Spokane, will move back into the state during the week, the DEQ update stated. It also ended on a hopeful note, saying moisture could be returning to Montana in the near future.
“This moisture could help to ease fire behavior and reduce smoke production. However, this pattern shift to our weather is likely more than a week away,” the update says. “In the meantime, expect surface smoke from regional and local wildfires to impact air quality for the foreseeable future.”
Almost a dozen large fires were burning throughout Montana on Monday, though only one was estimated at more than 2,000 acres. The 6,029-acre Silvertip Fire, currently the state’s largest by size, is burning in a remote part of the Bob Marshall Wilderness. The fire is 0% contained, but access has been a challenge, a situation report for the fire said. 
The Elder 1 fire, burning near Frenchtown, was reportedly at 40% containment on Monday after firefighters were able to make significant progress on the fire late last week and during the weekend. No structures have been reported lost in that blaze, which had 319 personnel assigned to the fire and six helicopters working it Monday. 
The National Interagency Fire Center estimates the fire has cost $6.4 million to fight.
Evacuations were ordered in the Good Creek/Alder Creek area on the Skillet Fire, which is burning 15 miles west of Olney, near Stillwater Lake. The fire is near a 2023 burn area and a larger team took over command on Monday.
Access to the area is difficult and dangerous due to fallen trees from the December storms that caused damage and flooding in large swaths of northwestern Montana.
“Crews and equipment will engage the fire where the risk to responders is low, and the probability of success is high,” a Monday update from the Skillet Fire states.
Fire crews were also battling a fire in the Little Belt Mountains near Showdown Mountain Ski Resort. The Ant Park Fire is burning about seven miles from the resort.
Two fires in Beaverhead County — the Bobcat Lakes Fire and the Sand Creek Fire — were both threatening structures in the Beaverhead-Deer Lodge National Forest.
The Bobcat Lakes fire was estimated at 1,560 acres and the Sand Creek Fire was listed at 1,003 acres.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A former Providence mayor endorses Morales to take down the incumbent
description: When David Morales was elected to the State House in 2020, then-Providence Mayor Jorge Elorza called to congratulate him and invited the freshman lawmaker to meet the next day, offering advice about governing and public service.  Six years later, Elorza formally endorsed Morales’ bid to unseat Providence Mayor Brett Smiley. “If you’re a voter who […]
text:
Rep. David Morales speaks to reporters after receiving the endorsement of former Mayor Jorge Elorza, left,  on Aug. 3, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) When David Morales was elected to the State House in 2020, then-Providence Mayor Jorge Elorza called to congratulate him and invited the freshman lawmaker to meet the next day, offering advice about governing and public service. 
Six years later, Elorza formally endorsed Morales’ bid to unseat Providence Mayor Brett Smiley.
“If you’re a voter who knows we can and must have something better, if you want our city to head in a new direction, then David Morales is your candidate,” Elorza told reporters and Morales’ supporters gathered inside a restaurant in the city’s Silver Lake neighborhood Monday.
Elorza, who led Rhode Island’s capital city from 2015 to 2023, said he believes Morales is willing to challenge the status quo at a time when Democratic politics is in desperate need of change. The former mayor said party leadership has been stagnant and that he values new ideas, perspectives, people, and “frankly, a new generation.”
“And that’s exactly what David represents,” he said.
Since 2021, Morales has represented Providence’s House District 7 — which covers Providence’s Mount Pleasant, Valley, and Elmhurst neighborhoods. At the time he was elected, Morales was the youngest Latino state legislator in the nation.
Even after completing his third term on Smith Hill, the 27-year-old Morales is still the state’s youngest legislator.
Morales described Elorza as a mentor who has helped shape his approach to public service. He said their relationship grew through their work together, including securing state funding for Providence’s community libraries and passing legislation banning source-of-income discrimination against low-income housing voucher recipients.
“Between each of these initiatives and efforts that we fought for and delivered on, it was rooted in the belief that government should uplift and support the working people and families who call our city home,” Morales said.
The two also share a focus on making Providence more affordable.
Elorza, who has lived in the Silver Lake neighborhood for 20 years, said families like his could not possibly live in the city today.
“Cities such as Providence are more and more becoming homes only for the wealthy and well-connected elites,” he said.
Morales said creating a more affordable Providence starts with enacting a rent stabilization ordinance, which the City Council passed earlier this year before Smiley vetoed it. The proposal, which Elorza said he would have backed, sought to cap annual rent increases for certain properties at 4%.
Despite their shared focus on housing, Elorza and Morales do differ on education policy — particularly on charter school expansion.
Elorza, who now runs Democrats for Education Reform, has been a staunch supporter of expanding high-performing charter schools. Morales, who once worked for Achievement First, this year voted in support of a three-year moratorium on new charter school approvals across the state.
Morales defended his vote when asked by a reporter, arguing it provides stability as Providence regains control of its schools after seven years of direct state oversight.
“In this moment it’s critical to ensure that we’re supporting our existing charter schools while making sure that our traditional public schools are receiving the support that they’re going to need to head into the next academic year,” he said.
But it’s because of education policy that an organization headed by the co-chairman of Elorza’s transition team issued its own endorsement for Smiley Monday afternoon.
“Families and children in Providence need a leader who believes that access to a good education should not be a privilege and that families are a key partner in their children’s schooling,” Victor Capellan, founder and CEO of Collective Action for Education, said in a statement.
Smiley’s campaign pushed back against Elorza’s endorsement, arguing Morales represents a return to the challenges the city faced under the former mayor’s administration.
“We need to move forward, not backward, and Mayor Smiley is running to continue building on the substantial progress Providence has made over the past four years,” Josh Block, a spokesperson for Smiley’s campaign, said in an emailed statement.
Elorza doesn’t see his tenure that way.
“I left the city, in my humble opinion, in perhaps the best shape that a mayor had inherited in over 50 years,” he said.
Matthew Ulricksen, an associate professor of political science at the Community College of Rhode Island, found Elorza’s endorsement of the insurgent Morales somewhat puzzling. Morales in May was endorsed by progressive U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders.
“If you’re trying to paint yourself as this outsider trying to come in and shake the system up, it’s not very revolutionary then to be endorsed by the establishment,” he said.
Ulricksen said it’s possible Elorza’s endorsement could sway some undecided voters to give Morales a second look, but the former mayor’s backing will only go so far if the campaign continues to avoid advertising.
“Money is the mother’s milk of politics,” he said. “If you don’t have money, it’s harder to communicate your message.”
Morales ended the second-quarter with a little over $125,000 in his campaign account. Smiley had over $1.2 million on hand at the end of June, which has allowed his campaign to dominate Rhode Island’s airwaves.
Filings made with the Federal Communications Commission shows Smiley has purchased over $411,000 worth of ad time since his first ad debuted July 9.
Morales said in an interview after the press conference he has no plans to air ads on television, instead sticking to investments in digital communications, mailers, and door knocking.
“While the mayor and his consultants can continue to waste their money, we will not,” he said.
Early voting begins Aug. 20 ahead of the Sept. 9 primary.

name: VTDigger
title: Pro-Aly Richards super PAC launches big ad buy late in Democratic governor primary
description:
The organization, which is not affiliated with Richards’ campaign, has spent more than $200,000 on ads in recent days, drawing criticism from her opponent, Amanda Janoo.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Pro-Aly Richards super PAC launches big ad buy late in Democratic governor primary.
text:
Aly Richards, democratic candidate for governor, speaks during a housing forum in South Burlington on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell
A political action committee backing Aly Richards in this year’s Democratic primary for Vermont governor has injected more than $200,000 into the race just weeks before election day.
The PAC, called Time for a Change, is not affiliated with Richards’ campaign. But the organization spent large sums in recent days on digital advertisements and text messages urging people to vote for her, according to newly-filed financial disclosures and screenshots of the mass media push reviewed by VTDigger.
The outside spending has become a flashpoint in the race. Richards’ opponent, Amanda Janoo, fired off a press release Friday suggesting that it made Richards look hypocritical because Richards said in a Vermont Public debate last month that she is “happy to not accept PAC money.”
Time for a Change is registered with the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office as an “independent expenditure-only” PAC. Under state law, these organizations, often called  “super PACs,” can raise an unlimited amount of money in support of a candidate but cannot coordinate with that candidate or contribute directly to their campaign.
Richards said as much in a statement posted to her social media on Friday, writing, “this group isn’t something I asked for, had knowledge of, or can control.” 
She described her campaign as “a grassroots movement of Vermonters who are committed to a brighter future for our state,” and that is “focused on continuing to build that movement and talking to as many Vermonters as possible.”
Angela Arsenault, a spokesperson for Richards’ campaign, referred VTDigger to that statement Monday in response to a request for an interview.
Janoo, in her press release, described the super PAC rules as a loophole in campaign finance law that she thinks is emblematic of “the sad state of politics.” She criticized how the PAC’s fundraising, which totaled $230,025 as of an Aug. 1 filing, came from just five large contributors. Only one of those donors was listed with an in-state address.
“It’s so clear to me how this system is designed by rich people,” Janoo said in an interview, speaking about campaign finance, adding that the system provides “a huge benefit for those who have connections.”
The PAC’s treasurer, John Hollar, said in an interview that Richards did not ask him or anyone else involved in the organization to raise or spend money on her behalf. He said the organization was created last month by “friends and supporters” of Richards.
Hollar is a former Montpelier mayor and former lobbyist with the firm Downs Rachlin Martin. He also served on the board of the Let’s Grow Kids Action Network, the sister organization of the pro-childcare lobbying group, Let’s Grow Kids, that Richards helmed for a decade before running for governor. 
Both entities provided the driving force behind a 2023 law creating a new payroll tax to bolster state subsidies for families in need of childcare. 
“We’ve had no communication with Aly or her campaign about anything,” Hollar said.
Still, the funding likely gives Richards a boost ahead of the Aug. 11 primary. The money the PAC has raised, $230,025, amounts to just over half of what Richards’ campaign has raised so far, according to the latest financial reports. As of Aug. 1, Richards’ campaign has raised $439,145; Janoo’s has raised $303,407, filings show.
The influx of advertising could help improve Richards’ name recognition in a race in which a majority of likely primary voters said they did not know enough about either her or Janoo to say which candidate they would vote for, recent polling found.
The Aug. 1 filing by Time for a Change lists two individuals and three organizations as its contributors, all of which donated between July 22 and 27.
Carl Ferenbach, co-founder of the Boston private equity firm Berkshire Partners and a co-founder of Let’s Grow Kids, donated $25,000. Tom MacLeay, former CEO of the Montpelier-based insurance company National Life Group, donated $5,000. 
MacLeay served on the board of Let’s Grow Kids and is the sole contributor with a Vermont address listed in the pro-Richards PAC’s filing. 
The largest single contribution, $100,000, came from a Missouri-based organization called Family Security and Prosperity. An organization with the same name, though with a Washington, D.C., address, is registered with the Federal Election Commission as a “hybrid PAC,” a type of political committee that operates similarly to a super PAC.
Impact Fellows Action Fund, a Kansas-based nonprofit organization that provided financial backing to Let’s Grow Kids, contributed $75,000 to the pro-Richards PAC. And another $25,000 came from a federally-registered hybrid PAC called “Government That Works PAC,” which was “established to defeat ineffective and extreme incumbent candidates,” according to its online donation page. The PAC has raised about $15 million over the 2026 election cycle so far, according to its filings with the FEC.
This year’s Democratic gubernatorial primary winner will face Republican Gov. Phil Scott in November. 
Hollar said he was not aware of any specific reasons why all of those people and organizations were contributing to Time for a Change other than the fact that “Aly is very well known in the world of childcare advocacy for the work that she’s done.”
The PAC’s media purchases are dated July 30 and 31. They include $141,500 of “online advertising,” according to filings, and $60,000 of “text messaging.” Another $8,500, for media “consulting,” is dated July 29.
Hollar said the fact the ad buys are late in the race was a result of when organizations contacted him and others with the intention of supporting Richards. Hollar added that he rejected the notion that it was a coordinated effort to sway the election late in the game.
Asked about Janoo’s assertion that the PAC spending was out of step with Richards’ comments at the Vermont Public debate, he reiterated that the organization was following campaign finance law.
“It’s simply an opportunity for these donors to provide the support that the law allows,” he said. “These are the rules that we have.”
Disclosure: Time for a Change is an advertiser with VTDigger.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Zay fired from utility regulator panel weeks after AES hike demotion
description: Gov. Mike Braun fired Indiana Utility Regulatory Commissioner Andy Zay from his post, in the first such dismissal in more than a decade.
text:
Andy Zay, then the chair of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, leads a daylong utility affordability hearing on March 24, 2026, at the IURC's downtown Indianapolis headquarters. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Gov. Mike Braun fired Indiana Utility Regulatory Commissioner Andy Zay from his post on Monday — just six weeks after Zay voted in favor of an AES Indiana rate hike and was demoted from IURC chair.
“Zay was discharged from employment with the State of Indiana today, August 3, 2026, for non-adherence to state policies and laws related to his role as Commissioner at the IURC,” agency spokesman Kirollos Barsoum said in an email to the Capital Chronicle.
More specifically, SPD said Zay was dismissed for “multiple potential violations of state policy; including failing to file a required financial disclosure after his removal as Chair, improperly awarding payments and personal gifts to employees, and directing staff to alter a public meeting agenda without consulting the new Chair.”
When reached by phone, Zay only said, “I cannot comment at this time.”
The firing is the latest shakeup to a typically quiet panel of regulators, and could impact a critical vote to reconsider the AES Indiana increase.
Braun first appointed Zay to the IURC — and named him chair — in December as part of the governor’s affordability push. Zay left a seat in the Indiana Senate in January to start the new gig.
In February, he launched an affordability inquiry, questioning the “big five” investor-owned utilities on their rates in March and holding a listening tour for frustrated ratepayers around the state through April.
State’s ratepayer advocate asks regulators to reconsider $71M AES rate hike

But in June, Zay joined Commissioners David Veleta and David Ziegner in a 3-1 vote to approve a $71 million rate electricity rate increase for AES Indiana customers. Commissioner Bob Deig voted in opposition, while a fifth member, Anthony Swinger, recused himself from the case.
The amount was less than the $193 million hike AES Indiana originally sought, and below the $91 million proposed in a settlement agreement.
But Braun and Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray — who had recommended a decrease to current rates — denounced the decision. Gray’s office represents ratepayers in IURC cases.
Days later, Braun removed Zay as chair and elevated Swinger, a former member of Gray’s office, to the IURC’s top spot.
“I thought I was fairly clear when I said I want you (commissioners) to make sure you’re changing the dynamic, to where you’re not rubber-stamping what utilities have wanted,” Braun told reporters at the time. “… I made the adjustment there in terms of the chairmanship, because I thought that should have been clear.”
The termination marks a rare step for an Indiana governor. IURC members are appointed to four-year terms and can leave voluntarily at any time — but can only be fired “for cause.”
Gov. Mitch Daniels carried out the most recent firing in 2012, when he dismissed former IURC Chair David Lott Hardy for his role in an ethics scandal, The Indiana Lawyer reported. Hardy was aware that an administrative law judge had been communicating with Duke Energy while presiding over its cases, ultimately getting a high-paying job with the utility.
Membership changes could impact AES hike reconsideration
Zay’s not the only one out as a regulator in more recent months.
Veleta announced he would resign from the IURC in late June. Braun selected a successor, attorney Joby Jerrells, in July after a nominating committee winnowed 25 applicants to three finalists.
“I think he could see that it was maybe going to be going in a little (bit of a) different direction,” Braun said of Veleta.
At the governor’s behest, the Office of Utility Consumer Counselor last month asked IURC members to reconsider their approval of the AES Indiana hike. The filing contends regulators “erred” in granting some of the utility’s requests.
The vote on that petition is scheduled for Wednesday, according to a finalized agenda posted Monday.
Jerrells will replace Veleta — who was one of the “yes” votes in June — and Zay’s spot will be vacant.
That leaves Ziegner as the only commissioner remaining who previously voted in favor of the increase.
The nominating committee, meanwhile, will reconvene to help fill its fifth vacancy in less than a year.
Indiana Democratic Party Chair Karen Tallian said “Braun is using Andy Zay as a scapegoat. Braun knew the AES case was being investigated when he appointed Zay. The buck must stop with the governor’s poor judgment. The only commissioner who voted against any recent major electric increase is former Democratic State Senator Bob Deig. We invite Hoosiers to elect more Democratic legislators this November who will put families before utility profits for a change.”

name: WyoFile
title: Colorado River plan spares Wyoming from major cuts
description:
Water managers would still heavily rely on Flaming Gorge as tool to prevent Lake Powell and Lake Mead from reaching critically low levels.
The post Colorado River plan spares Wyoming from major cuts appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming and other Upper Colorado River Basin states would be spared mandatory cuts, while the Lower Basin states — Arizona, Nevada and California — face significant water use reductions under a new federal proposal for future management of the beleaguered western water system.
The U.S. Department of the Interior issued Friday its final environmental impact statement, guiding how water will be divided during a shortage. The rare federal intervention came after stakeholder states and tribes failed, so far, to agree on a plan of their own. The current drought contingency plan, which is intended to prevent Lake Powell and Lake Mead from shrinking below “minimum power pool” — the point where water releases won’t flow through electric-generating turbines — expires at the end of this year.





Click to enlarge: The Colorado River Basin, shown as upper and lower basins. (Bureau of Reclamation)

The new federal plan, administered by the Bureau of Reclamation, could force an annual reduction of 3 million acre-feet of water consumed by Lower Basin states, depending on the severity of the water shortage. Upper Basin states avoid mandatory cuts — at least in the short-term — but would have to collectively conserve up to 200,000 acre-feet annually. The plan also calls on Flaming Gorge Reservoir, which straddles the Wyoming-Utah border, to remain a primary backup, potentially tapped for up to 1 million acre-feet of extra annual water releases, according to federal documents.
Federal officials appear to have been swayed by a particular argument from the Upper Basin states regarding the split in water-use reductions, according to some analysts. Because they are headwater states, their farmers, ranchers and other water users already suffer significant cutbacks in times of drought because they generally get what Mother Nature delivers, whereas the Lower Basin states reap the benefits of balancing deliveries via a network of reservoir storage. 
“While the final details are still being analyzed by Upper Division States, we are encouraged that new operating guidelines will better reflect existing water supply, which must underpin any practicable plan going forward,” Gov. Mark Gordon and his fellow Upper Basin state governors said in a joint statement Friday.
Wyoming State Engineer Brandon Gebhart put a finer point on the division of the federal government’s and Mother Nature’s authorities.
“In the Upper Basin, water use is already limited by available supply, administered under state law, and the Secretary [of Interior] does not have comparable authority to mandate reductions,” Gebhart told WyoFile via email. “That does not mean the Upper Basin has no responsibilities — it means those responsibilities are carried out through different mechanisms, including reservoir operations, state-led programs and collaborative efforts to maintain system reliability.”
Wyoming and the other Upper Basin states are advancing water conservation efforts to improve long-term resilience for the river system, Gebhart added.
Historically low snowpack this past winter, combined with a searing heat wave across much of the West, has wreaked havoc on the Colorado River system, sapping it to just 32% capacity, according to federal data. Lake Powell measured 23% capacity on Sunday while Lake Mead measured 27%.
Lake Powell is expected to continue shrinking this year, despite reduced releases and extra flows from upstream Flaming Gorge, according to the Bureau of Reclamation.
“The combined contents of Lake Powell and Lake Mead have not been this low since before Glen Canyon Dam began filling in 1963, and since 2000 water use has exceeded total system inflow in most years,” the agency stated in a press release Friday.




Click to enlarge: This chart depicts Flaming Gorge Reservoir’s water level since October 2025. (Bureau of Reclamation) 
In coordination with the Upper Basin states, the bureau announced in April it would release up to 1 million additional acre-feet of water from Flaming Gorge through April 2027. At the time, water managers predicted the extra release would drop the reservoir by about 35 feet to a capacity of 59%.
Barring a last-minute agreement among Colorado River stakeholders, the Interior is expected to issue a record of decision later this year that would put into motion a 10-year drought contingency plan.
“We are witnessing the lowest reservoir levels in the Colorado River System’s history and there is no guarantee regarding the future water supply,” Gordon and his Upper Basin counterparts said in a prepared statement. “Today’s framework does not represent a final solution, but enables the river to be managed in the short-term while the seven states and [Department of Interior] continue to negotiate a consensus solution.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Record heat and dewpoints recorded across Iowa
description: July ended with hot temperatures and record high dew point temperatures, according to a weekly weather report from the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship.  While the temperatures were warm and parts of the state could use some rain as of the July 27 through Aug. 2 reporting period, Iowa’s crops continue to progress […]
text:
Soybeans in July. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) July ended with hot temperatures and record high dew point temperatures, according to a weekly weather report from the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship. 
While the temperatures were warm and parts of the state could use some rain as of the July 27 through Aug. 2 reporting period, Iowa’s crops continue to progress closely to the average pace as reported by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to State Climatologist Justin Glisan, Iowa had slightly above average rainfall for the week, with a statewide average of 1.31 inch, while the normal is nine-tenths of an inch. The eastern half of the state received heavy rain during the period, with areas logging accumulation totals between 1.5 inches and 8 inches for the week. 
Glisan reported that temperatures tapered off late in the week, despite sitting in the “unseasonably warm” category for most of the reporting period. According to Glisan, the average temperature statewide was 76.6 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 3.6 degrees above the normal. 
Per the weather report, “numerous” Iowa airports logged record dew-point temperatures July 26. Burlington Municipal Airport in Des Moines County recorded a dew point temperature of 85 degrees and a high temperature of 92 degrees, making for a heat index of 121 degrees.
A weather station in Little Sioux logged the highest air temperature for the week at 102 degrees, which Glisan said was also the warmest temperature recorded in the state this year. 
The temperatures might have made it sweaty out in the field, but farmers had 5.7 days suitable for field work during the reporting period, according to USDA’s crop progress and condition report.


Crop phenological stages:
— Corn in dough stage: a thick or dough-like substance is present in all kernels.
— Corn in dent stage: all the kernels have dented, ear is firm and no milk is present in the kernels.
— Soybeans setting pods: pods are developing on lower portions of the plant, with some blooming still on top of plant. 


All but 7% of Iowa’s corn acres reached the silking stage by the end of the reporting period, which is 2 percentage points ahead of the year prior and the five-year average.
Four percent of corn acres reached the dent stage in Iowa, which is half of the amount from the year prior, but just 2 percentage points behind the five-year average. 
Corn acres in the dough stage continued to sit slightly behind the 2025 crop’s pace and slightly ahead of the five-year average with 48% of the crop in the dough stage as of Sunday. 
Corn condition rated 80% good to excellent and soybean condition was 78% good to excellent for the reporting period. 
Nearly 90% of soybeans acres are blooming in Iowa, putting the crop on pace with the 2025 soybean crop. Just over 60% of soybean acres were setting pods as of the reporting period. At 61%, the crop is 2 percentage points behind last year and the average. 
The majority of oat acres — 87% — have been harvested, according to the report, which rated the crop as 82% good to excellent. 
Abnormally dry conditions increased from 36% of the state the week prior to 46% of the state in the most recent weekly report from the U.S. Drought Monitor. Most of the dry conditions, including 22% of the state in moderate drought conditions, are on the western side of the state. 
Sixty percent of topsoil was rated as having adequate moisture and 25% of topsoil moisture was rated as short for the period. Subsoil moisture rated 58% adequate and 27% short. 
According to 30-day maps from the state, most of Iowa accumulated less rain than what is typical in July, though parts of central and eastern Iowa received between 1 and 4 inches more than the normal. Average temperatures across the state were between 1 and 3 degrees warmer during July 2026 than the normal.

title: Democratic challengers Foulkes and Khamsyvoravong widen cash leads over incumbents in Q2
description: With less than a month before early voting begins for Rhode Island state and local primaries, candidates are pounding the pavement and packing in the public events in the hopes of gaining voters’ support — and potentially, donations.  Second-quarter campaign finance reports were due to the Rhode Island Board of Elections by 11:59 p.m. on […]
text:
With the primary election fast approaching, second quarter campaign finance reports show wide gaps in the amount of cash on hand between challengers and incumbents in the race for governor and lieutenant governor. (Photo by Nolan Page/Rhode Island Current)With less than a month before early voting begins for Rhode Island state and local primaries, candidates are pounding the pavement and packing in the public events in the hopes of gaining voters’ support — and potentially, donations. 
Second-quarter campaign finance reports were due to the Rhode Island Board of Elections by 11:59 p.m. on July 31. Here’s a look at how state general office candidates fared in fundraising and spending during the three-month period that ended June 30. Candidates who are participating in the Sept. 9 primary will have to file two more campaign reports before voting day: one on Aug. 12, reflecting donations and fundraising from July 1 to Aug. 11; and a second on Sept. 2, reflecting donations and fundraising from Aug. 12 to Sept. 1.
Early voting begins Aug. 20. 
Left to right are Gov. Dan McKee; his Democratic rival Helena Buonanno Foulkes; independent Ken Block; Republican Aaron Guckian and Republican Elaine Pelino. (McKee, Foulkes and Guckian photos by Michael Salerno; contributed photo by Block; Pelino photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)
Governor’s race 
Democratic challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes continues to outraise Gov. Dan McKee, with more than four times the cash on hand, though that includes a $1.8 million loan balance from several years ago. Independent Ken Block bolstered his first quarter of fundraising with a $10,250 personal loan. Republicans Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino brought in just over $11,000 between them, with Pelino spending less than 10% of the $61,000 Guckian reported in campaign expenditures.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Fargo Mayor Josh Boschee resigns from North Dakota Senate
description: New Fargo Mayor Josh Boschee announced his resignation from the North Dakota Senate on Monday, effective as of Aug. 4. Boschee was elected mayor in June and took office last month.  In a letter addressed to Senate Majority Leader Sen. David Hogue, chair of Legislative Management, Boschee said he resigned earlier than he had originally […]
text:
Sen. Josh Boschee, D-Fargo, speaks on the Senate floor on March 13, 2025, during debate on a resolution that urges the overturning of same-sex marriage. (Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)New Fargo Mayor Josh Boschee announced his resignation from the North Dakota Senate on Monday, effective as of Aug. 4.
Boschee was elected mayor in June and took office last month. 
In a letter addressed to Senate Majority Leader Sen. David Hogue, chair of Legislative Management, Boschee said he resigned earlier than he had originally planned so the District 44 Democratic-NPL executive committee would be able to name a replacement to participate in the newly announced special session of the Legislature on Sept. 2 to address banning kratom.
Jessie Smette, chair of the Dem-NPL District 44 executive committee, said the process to appoint a replacement for Boschee has already been completed and the district expects to name his replacement later in the week.
Gov. Armstrong announces special session, emergency actions to ban kratom in North Dakota

Since Boschee’s resignation occurred within 94 days of the next general election, under North Dakota state law, his replacement will be able to serve in the North Dakota Senate through 2028, which is when Boschee’s term would have expired.
Smette said a form seeking potential replacements was posted to the district’s social media page for much of the past month and the form was also sent out to members of the district’s email list. Several responded, she said, and the executive committee met last week to make its selection.
Boschee was elected to the North Dakota House in 2012 and would go on to become the Democratic caucus leader in the chamber before being named House minority leader in 2019, a position he would keep for the next four years. 
He was elected to the North Dakota Senate in 2024 after former Sen. Merrill Piepkorn decided to run for governor. He served as assistant minority leader in the Senate during the 2025 legislative session.
“Serving my downtown and north Fargo neighbors over the past 14 years has been one of the greatest honors of my life,” Boschee wrote. “Although stepping away from the Legislature is not an easy decision, I do so with tremendous optimism for North Dakota’s future.”
He said he plans to continue working with state lawmakers over the next four years as mayor of Fargo.
Rep. Josh Boschee, D-Fargo, speaks during a meeting of the Legislative Procedure and Arrangements Committee on March 20, 2024. (Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Boschee was the first openly gay member of the Legislature in North Dakota.
Dem-NPL Senate Minority Leader Sen. Kathy Hogan said Boschee listened, studied, had a gift relating to people and was able to work with people of different points of view on a regular basis.
“He is a model public servant because it was never about Josh and he doesn’t care if he gets credit,” Hogan said. “Everybody likes Josh and I think that’s because Josh loves everybody else.”
She said Boschee was instrumental in bringing the issue of North Dakota homelessness to the forefront and passed a resolution in 2023 directing state lawmakers to identify barriers in state programs and policy for people to become housing stable.
Smette said Boschee was a “true servant leader,” and his open communication with constituents was one of the reasons she decided to get more involved at the district level.
“It’s a huge win for Fargo to have Josh as our mayor and we were lucky to have him as a senator in our district as well,” she said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lexington residents settle lawsuits against police department and ex-chiefs
description: Lexington residents hold up signs at a Jan. 6, 2026, mayor and board of aldermen meeting, calling on the city to respond to the Department of Justice findings regarding problems with the police department.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Residents and visitors who sued Lexington police have settled their federal lawsuits over what they alleged was a pattern of misconduct including excessive force, unlawful search and seizures, retaliatory arrests and detentions without due process, the ACLU of Mississippi announced Monday.
Amounts of the settlement were not disclosed, and the deal came with no admission or finding of liability or wrongdoing by the defendants, according to the ACLU. The lawsuits were against the city, the police department, several named officers and former police chiefs Sam Dobbins and Charles Henderson. 
“Police hold a powerful role in our society. While performing that role, they must balance enforcing the law and protecting constitutional rights. This settlement helps achieve that balance for the LPD, our clients and the residents of Lexington,” Joshua Tom, legal director at the ACLU of Mississippi, said in a statement. 
One plaintiff, Deborah Powell, alleged in her 2024 lawsuit that in her 2024 lawsuit that Lexington officers threw her to the ground and put her in jail for days just for trying to get a court-ordered reimbursement from the police department. 
Javarius Russell, who is also a law enforcement officer, alleged in his 2023 lawsuit that police arrested him for a vehicle crash he said didn’t happen and jailed him over a long weekend. Former chief Dobbins told him if he paid $2,700, he would be released and the charges dropped.
Plaintiff Andrial Young alleged in his 2024 lawsuit that officers stopped his car saying that he failed to wear a seatbelt, but he had one on. Officers claimed they smelled marijuana and asked to search his vehicle. Young declined the search, leading officers to remove him and search the car, anyway. They did not find any illegal substances. After the search, officers arrested Young and detained him for hours at the police station. 
On Monday, the three plaintiffs said the settlement, which was signed off on by the court, has brought them some justice. 
“I hope this settlement helps Lexington improve its policing in the future,” Young said. 
Dobbins was Lexington’s chief until his 2022 firing days after the Mississippi Center for Investigative Reporting first reported him using racist and homophobic language when he bragged about killing multiple people while working as a law enforcement officer. 
Henderson, Dobbins’ second in command, became the new police chief and served until January of this year, when his certification was suspended due to a violation of the Law Enforcement Code of Ethics. The alleged violation took place in Jackson in November 2024 when Henderson worked for the Jackson Police Department. 
Lexington went through two interim police chiefs before hiring David Simmons in May. 
In 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice opened a pattern and practice investigation into the Lexington police and its investigation report detailing the department’s violations of the First, Fourth and 14th Amendments. The DOJ found Lexington police jailed people for unpaid fines without determining whether people could afford to pay, resulting in a “two-tiered system of justice.” 
This year, the Lexington Board of Aldermen adopted some Justice Department recommendations, including efforts to ensure officers who make stops, searches and arrests are authorized to use force with clear direction, that they have sufficient training and supervision and that the department improves record-keeping to hold officers accountable for inappropriate or unlawful conduct. 
The ACLU of Mississippi partnered with law firms Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP, O’Melveny & Myers, and Morgan, Lewis & Bockius LLP, which worked on the lawsuits pro bono. 
Craig C. Martin, lead counsel for Willkie, said the settlement shows clients’ courage, the team’s hard work and a chance to restore trust and integrity in Lexington.
The Lexington lawsuits were part of the ACLU of Missisisppi’s Police Accountability Initiative, which focuses on police violence, racial discrimination and unconstitutional policing practices around the state through litigation, advocacy and partnerships. 
In the Monday statement, the ACLU of Mississippi said it will continue work on police accountability and reform and its support of people affected by unconstitutional policing.  police accountability and reform and its support of community members affected by unconstitutional policing.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lindstrom turns in signatures, releases ‘Nebraska Doctrine’ for nonpartisan governor bid
description: Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom submitted more than 5,700 signatures in his bid to qualify as a nonpartisan candidate for Nebraska governor.
text:
Former State Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, 2026 nonpartisan candidate for Nebraska governor. (Photo courtesy of the Lindstrom campaign)LINCOLN — Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha submitted more than 5,700 signatures Monday in his bid to appear on the ballot as a nonpartisan candidate for Nebraska governor this November.
Over the weekend, he also unveiled his policy platform, which he calls the “Nebraska Doctrine.”
Lindstrom, 45, would need more than 4,000 valid signatures, of which at least 750 signatures apiece must come from each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts, to qualify for the ballot. If so, he and running mate Mike Picard of Omaha, a Navy veteran who is club director and head coach of ENVY Volleyball Club, would be the fourth gubernatorial ticket this November.
“Nebraskans signed these petitions because they know something is wrong and they’re tired of being told everything is fine,” Lindstrom said in a statement.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, bottom left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, bottom right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party, top left, and registered nonpartisan former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, top right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“In three and a half years, this administration has spent through a historic cash reserve, raided cash funds and made billions in commitments with no sustainable way to pay for them,” Lindstrom continued. “Now Nebraskans are being handed the bill.”
Local election officials will verify county-specific voter signatures in the coming weeks.
If qualified, Lindstrom would face Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, 70, a Republican who beat Lindstrom for the GOP gubernatorial nomination in 2022; former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, 63, whom Lindstrom served with for six years; and Rick Beard of Omaha, 58, a wine professional, private chef and Legal Marijuana NOW nominee.
The Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office must certify the Nov. 3 ballot by Sept. 11. Finalized ballots must be mailed to overseas and military voters by the following week.
Opponents respond
The Republican and Democratic campaigns for Nebraska governor this year have each portrayed Lindstrom as either more conservative or more liberal than his nonpartisan label would suggest. Meanwhile, Beard, the existing third-party candidate, has welcomed Lindstrom.
Taylor Sliva, Pillen’s campaign manager, said in a Monday statement that Pillen is the “only commonsense conservative in this race” and is working “relentlessly” to deliver “real” property tax relief, keep communities safe, protect babies and make life more affordable.
“Lindstrom’s record aligns more with liberal policies — raising gas taxes, supporting giveaways for illegal aliens and his friends and supporting soft-on-crime policies — than Nebraska’s conservative values,” Sliva told the Nebraska Examiner. “He’s a failed career politician who will do and say anything to see his name on the ballot again and again.”
Pillen talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

Walz’s campaign a few weeks ago had blasted Lindstrom as a “lifelong conservative Republican” whose “record speaks for itself: he is no moderate.” But on Monday, Walz took a more measured tone.
“Even though more candidates are entering the race, my focus is staying the same,” Walz said. “It’s always been about lowering costs for working families and growing our state.”
Beard told the Examiner that he thinks it’s “great” that Lindstrom got the signatures. Beard hopes Lindstrom pushes “out-of-the-box thinking” and embraces the “massive revenue” that a functional medical cannabis program could bring, for instance.
“Nebraska is in DEEP trouble financially and the more ideas and concepts we have about fixing it the better,” Beard said in a Monday email. “I also look forward to having  a candidate that will debate me and push new thinking for leadership that is currently failing us.”
Lindstrom, speaking with the Examiner shortly before the May 12 primary, had said part of his calculus for jumping into the race at the time was what he viewed as an uphill climb for Walz as a Democrat, worried that it “probably still mathematically isn’t there in the state.”
The last non-Republican to represent Nebraska was former Gov. Ben Nelson, a Democrat who served between 1991 and 1999 and then served two terms in the U.S. Senate, between 2001 and 2013. He was the last Democrat elected statewide, too, in his 2006 reelection bid.
Walz has said she hasn’t heard concerns about her political party, while Pillen’s team has leaned into Nebraska’s conservative record.
The ‘Nebraska Doctrine’
Lindstrom said in his policy documents released in the past couple of days that he believes Nebraska’s problem has never been a shortage of land, work or ambition but that the good life is unaffordable for those who grew up in Nebraska.
“Government’s job is to fix the conditions causing that — not to win the argument about it,” the “Nebraska Doctrine” states.
Walz talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

His main ideas, if elected, are to take pressure off property taxes and make property valuations possible to plan around, build housing where jobs already are, protect public power and expand the energy grid before demand outruns it, keep more of what Nebraska grows getting processed in Nebraska and finish deploying broadband for rural internet.
“Nebraska can be the best place in America to build a life — not by becoming another state, but by becoming the strongest version of itself,” the platform states. “The Nebraska Doctrine rejects grievance, division and short-term politics, and chooses opportunity, stability and long-term thinking instead. It is a call to build.”
Property taxes and property valuations
Property taxes remain a key component of Lindstrom’s platform, with him calling for direct changes to how county assessors could value property and how schools could levy taxes.
Lindstrom suggests moving all major classes of property toward rolling valuation averaging, which his documents state would “damp volatility” while remaining compliant to the Nebraska Constitution’s requirement that all property be valued uniformly. He also wants to reduce the maximum property tax authority for school operating expenses from $1.05 per $100 of property valuation to 50 cents over time, while increasing state support “as fiscal capacity allows.”
Specifically regarding agricultural valuations, Lindstrom also calls to transition to a system that places greater emphasis on productive value. 
Beard talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

The long-term objective would be to value ag land instead of at 75% market value to approximately 80% of productive net income and 20% market value. Land categories could be valued accordingly, such as for row crop, irrigated and dryland production, pasture, grazing land, hay ground, horticultural uses and specialized classifications.
Lindstrom said using data models, such as from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the University of Nebraska, would also introduce predictability.
“Reform of this kind is a transition, not an event,” Lindstrom’s doctrine states. “Each step should be tested for constitutional compliance, fiscal sustainability, and real taxpayer relief, and paced to growth and budget discipline rather than promised on a schedule that cannot survive a downturn. That is slower than a slogan. It is also the only version that lasts.”
Other proposals
Lindstrom also wants to grow Nebraska by aggressively recruiting former Nebraskans home and encouraging industries to choose the Cornhusker State, while also building homes near existing infrastructure and jobs and investing in regional growth hubs.
He would also encourage coordination among K-12 schools, community colleges, apprenticeships and employers to serve as “one coordinated pipeline.”
Former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, 2026 nonpartisan candidate for Nebraska governor, meets with voters in fall 2025. (Photo courtesy of the Lindstrom campaign)
Lindstrom said recruitment should come where the state has “real advantages rather than chasing whatever is fashionable,” specifically naming agriculture and food processing, advanced manufacturing, logistics, insurance and financial services, energy, digital infrastructure, healthcare, and defense-adjacent industries.
Lindstrom says artificial intelligence also deserves “neither panic nor hype” but should be governed by transparency, privacy and accountability and be adopted where it “demonstrably helps” and left alone where not.
His doctrine suggests that state government should rebrand talks away from data centers as a headline to discuss digital infrastructure, secure cloud services, advanced computing capacity, cybersecurity and AI infrastructure.
Lindstrom also has a broader goal, which he calls “The Arena Project,” to identify and support “emerging leaders” across business, agriculture, education, nonprofits, local government and public service.
“The Arena Project should encourage people to participate constructively rather than remain silent or disengaged,” the Doctrine states.
Nonpartisan candidates
Lindstrom filed his petition effort July 13, becoming the sixth nonpartisan Nebraskan to launch an effort for the 2026 cycle. He’s the third to submit signatures, following Dan Osborn of Omaha for U.S. Senate and Mark Cohen of Lemoyne for Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District.
Former State Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, left, talks with University of Nebraska Regent Jim Scheer of Norfolk, a former state senator and legislative speaker who served with Lindstrom. June 6, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The deadline for anyone wishing to submit signatures for partisan races was 5 p.m. Monday. 
The deadline for candidates wishing to petition to be on the ballot for nonpartisan races, such as the Legislature, State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents, is 5 p.m. Sept. 1. No one is running signatures for those races, at least as of yet.
Lindstrom has repeatedly said he doesn’t want to play “spoiler” and repeated Monday he isn’t running a “protest campaign” or seeking to pull votes from anyone.
“Neither party is willing to tell Nebraskans the truth,” Lindstrom said. “You cannot cut your way to prosperity, and you cannot spend your way to growth. Nebraska doesn’t just have a budget problem — we have a leadership problem. Nebraska’s future is still ours to shape and the time to change course is now.”
The general election is Nov. 3.
